todays_goal: Use precise models, solve mixed percentage problems, and explain what evidence proves.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: September 8 work correctly computed test accuracy, chose the model with stronger generalization, explained why test accuracy matters, and identified the limitation of a small test set.
lessons.course_context: Progress from overall accuracy to understanding different types of classification mistakes.
learning_objectives: Classify predictions as true positive, false positive, false negative, or true negative.
Explain why equal accuracy can hide different error types.
lessons.why_it_matters: Accuracy alone does not describe how a model is wrong; understanding error types is important when different mistakes have different consequences.

vocabulary.definition: the model predicts a class is present when it is not
the model misses a class that is actually present
the model correctly identifies a class that is present
the model correctly rejects a class that is absent

lessons.written_instruction: Use one target class, CUP. Compare the actual object with the model prediction. False positive: predicts CUP for a non-cup. False negative: predicts NOT CUP for an actual cup.

worked_examples.title: False positive
worked_examples.explanation: The model predicted the target class even though the class was absent.

independent_practice.prompt: Actual: CUP. Prediction: CUP. Name the result type.
Actual: BOOK. Prediction: CUP. Name the result type for CUP.
Actual: CUP. Prediction: NOT CUP. Name the result type for CUP.
Actual: BOOK. Prediction: NOT CUP. Name the result type for CUP.
A test set has 20 images. The model gets 16 correct. What is the accuracy?
Why can two models with the same accuracy still make different kinds of mistakes?

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain the difference between a false positive and a false negative.
exit_ticket.answer: A false positive predicts the target class when it is absent; a false negative misses the target class when it is present.

exit_ticket.prompt: Give one real-world situation where a false negative could matter more than a false positive. Explain briefly.
exit_ticket.answer: Answers vary; example: a safety detector failing to detect an actual hazard could be more serious than a false alarm.

lessons.voice_prompt: Progress from accuracy to error types. Use CUP versus NOT CUP. Keep explanations to one or two sentences. For assigned questions, never give the label; ask Atticus what the actual object is and what the model predicted, then let him classify it.
